documents.abstract: This lecture for MSc students in aerospace engineering presents a workflow for research with AI agents, from the author's evaluation of large language models between ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 3, Gemini 3.1, and Claude Opus 5.5. A use case shows an agent building a verified and validated Abaqus model of the double cantilever beam benchmarks of Krueger (2008) in one morning, with the researcher answering the decisive questions at checkpoints. The lecture discusses the responsible use of AI, how AI changes highly technical work, the growing role of experiments, and what this means for junior engineers. Lecture Given on 19 October 2026 as part of the Aerospace Structures and Materials core, Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, Delft University of Technology, Delft, The Netherlands. Contents Motivation for this lecture: why, after evaluating the new large language models every summer, Claude Opus 5 (August 2026) changed the author's way of working, and why the lecture was given now. Learning objectives: understand, evaluate and apply the author's way of working with novel AI models; create your own way of working with them; re-evaluate the role of a junior engineer in a world with AI. A brief history of large language models: from GPT-1 (2018) to GPT-4 (2023). How AI entered my research/education workflows: ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 3, Gemini 3.1, Claude Opus 5 and Claude Opus 5.5, and an analogy of three kinds of helpers. What fits inside current LLMs: tokens, context windows measured in papers, parameters against context, and the context of one agent session. Responsible use of AI: three rules, with a discussion: "Everything that can be automated should be automated"; "Focus on the crucial things, avoid the trivial things"; "Never delegate the decisions that make your work yours". My workflow with AI: a working folder in an integrated development environment, Claude as the agent, an HPC cluster as the simulation environment, and the state of the work kept in files (README, DECISIONS, REPORT), not in the chat. Consequences of a workflow with AI: how research moves forward through verification, validation and new hypotheses; where AI can take over parts of this process; what changed in the author's work. Use case: a verified DCB model: the prompt (goal, ten ground rules, phases with checkpoints), one morning by the clock, and where the model stood at the end of it. Figures as code: TikZ: vector figures written by the agent from the models' own data. How has AI changed highly technical jobs: numerical work and theoretical research; the shift from executing calculations to synthesis and verification; why experiments matter more, including AI combined with mechanical testing. The AI workflow of a junior engineer: how engineers grew until about 2024, judging what the AI produces, and two discussions. Take-home messages. The use case The agent built an Abaqus model of the double cantilever beam (DCB) benchmarks of the NASA report by Krueger (2008), NASA/TM-2008-215123, following a prompt written as a contract: every value with its source, every analysis through scripts, failed runs kept, and stops at two checkpoints where the researcher decides. In one morning, the agent completed the environment check and the reference card (09:46 to 10:07), wrote the plan after the researcher's decisions at the first checkpoint (11:23 to 11:29), and built and verified the model after the second checkpoint: the first models ran at 12:07, and the model worked at 13:23. At that point, the unidirectional model agreed with the published Marc 3D results of Orifici and Krueger (2010) within 0.1 to 0.6 %, and with the 2008 report within 0.1 to 0.8 % once its crack fronts were taken 0.5 mm beyond the labelled lengths; the acceptance criterion of the approved plan was 2 %. Running the use case The file use-case.zip contains the prompt of the use case, PROMPT_use_case.md. The report it works from is not included; to run the use case: Download the report by Krueger (2008), NASA/TM-2008-215123, from the NASA Technical Reports Server, where it is available free of charge: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20080015439. In your project folder, create a subfolder named references and save the report there as references/krueger2008NASA.pdf. The file name is the key of the case: if the agent does not find this file, it stops and asks. Place the prompt in the project folder, and check that its cluster settings suit your environment: ground rule 4 submits every analysis with qsub, and Phase 0 loads Abaqus in the cluster. Open the project folder with an AI coding agent (in the lecture: Claude, in an integrated development environment), and ask it to read the prompt and start with Phase 0. The agent creates the case folder krueger2008NASA_dcb next to references, and stops at two checkpoints for your decisions. Requirements: Abaqus with a valid licence, including its Python for scripting and post-processing; a computer or cluster to run the analyses; and Python for the work outside Abaqus, such as digitising figures. Take-home messages Write the prompt as a contract: definitions, ground rules, phases, and checkpoints where the agent stops and asks. Keep the state in files (README, DECISIONS, REPORT), not in the chat: someone else can reproduce every number. Automate everything that can be automated, and keep the focus on the crucial things. Let the agent verify and look for evidence; you judge the evidence. Delegate the implementation and the evidence for verification; keep the validation, the new hypotheses and the decisions at the checkpoints. Numerical work is increasingly automated, and theory is reaching automated scale: the work shifts to synthesis and problem definition, and to verification and auditing, and experiments matter more. For junior engineers: invest in the fundamentals; make a real effort to check what the AI produces against independent references; if you are not sure about a decision, study and talk to more experienced peers. Questions for discussion What do you consider a responsible use of AI? Which tasks of your work are trivial, and which are crucial? Which decisions make your work yours? In the process of doing research, where do you think we can delegate to AI? How can a recently graduated student judge what the AI produces and answer the decisive questions? How can a junior engineer work in synthesis and problem definition, and in verification and auditing of what an AI model does and produces, without the experience of a senior engineer, and without the chance to gain it the conventional way? documents.abstract: This conceptual article explores practical ways in which college and university instructors can leverage artificial intelligence (AI) to support assessment as learning and develop students’ feedback literacy. Traditional assessment practices often focus on assessment for learning (informing instruction) or of learning (measuring outcomes), while assessment as learning—when students actively monitor and reflect on their own learning—receives less attention. AI can help instructors leverage assessment as a learning tool by generating work samples for student analysis and providing timely, actionable feedback that students can use to revise their work. When combined with instructor modeling, peer dialogue, and scaffolds such as guiding questions or graphic organizers, AI-supported feedback promotes metacognition, self-directed learning, and critical evaluation skills. The article provides practical guidance, including prompts and strategies for using AI to enhance student engagement with feedback, helping instructors create more efficient, effective, and student-centered practices that utilize assessments as learning tools.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support learning in higher education, but evidence regarding changes in students' academic self-efficacy, self-regulated learning, and academic engagement remains limited. This study examined changes associated with a six-week generative AI-based data analysis education program among students at a three-year college in Wuhan, Hubei Province, China. A one-group pretest-posttest design was employed. Of 210 questionnaires distributed, 202 valid paired responses were analyzed. Academic self-efficacy, self-regulated learning, and academic engagement were measured using five-point Likert scales, with adapted items informed by established instruments. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlations, and paired-samples t tests were conducted. All three outcomes increased significantly: academic self-efficacy from 3.21 to 3.48 (dz = 0.38), self-regulated learning from 3.18 to 3.52 (dz = 0.51), and academic engagement from 3.35 to 3.66 (dz = 0.44). Posttest correlations among the outcomes were positive (r = 0.56-0.65, all p < .001). These findings suggest that structured AI-supported data analysis instruction may accompany improvements in students' confidence, learning regulation, and engagement. However, the one-group design cannot isolate the causal contribution of generative AI from other elements of the instructional program. As artificial intelligence (AI) service agents increasingly simulate human interaction, the basis for distinguishing human service has become theoretically ambiguous. While prior research consistently identifies authenticity as a key limitation of AI-enabled service, authenticity remains underdeveloped as a uniquely human service capability. Addressing this gap, we introduce Authentic Relational Service (ARS) as a distinct form of service through which frontline employees create genuine, contextually responsive, and relationship-centered customer interactions. We further conceptualize authenticity as a competency-based capability and develop a measure of Authentic Relational Service Competency (ARSC), which enables frontline employees to enact ARS. Using established scale-development procedures, this study identifies and validates four dimensions of ARSC: perspective-taking, patience, creativity, and agility. By conceptualizing and operationalizing Authentic Relational Service as a distinct human service capability, this research advances theory on human-AI service differentiation and provides a foundation for understanding uniquely human value creation in service contexts.

Purpose This study examines how the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and students' creative thinking (CT) contribute to smart learning (SL) and academic performance (AP) in higher education. It further examines whether AI use and SL mediate the relationship between CT and AP in a sequential manner. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative approach was adopted, and data were collected from 227 university students in Bangladesh. Structural equation modelling with SmartPLS was used to evaluate the proposed relationships. Findings The results show that both AI usage and CT are positively and significantly related to SL and AP. Beyond these direct associations, the data also point to a meaningful serial mediation pathway: students with stronger CT tend to report greater AI usage, which is in turn associated with higher SL engagement, and this heightened engagement is associated with better AP. Originality/value This study uniquely links CT, AI use, SL and AP in Bangladeshi higher education. It shows how CT affects academic achievement through sequential paths of AI usage and SL, clarifying how student talents convert into outcomes in digital learning environments. The findings suggest that institutions should promote CT and use AI-based learning tools to improve student performance.

Proactive agents can support group collaboration by surfacing useful information without waiting to be asked, but even relevant contributions can be disruptive if poorly timed. In this work, we isolate the timing question: given a fixed candidate contribution such as a clarification or relevant fact, when should an AI agent chime in? We introduce PITCH (Proactive Intervention Timing in CHat), to our knowledge the first benchmark with large-scale human judgments of proactive agent timing collected from participants in the same unscripted multi-party conversations they took part in. To collect high-quality judgments, we design a novel interface in which 2-4 people chat synchronously, author candidate AI contribution messages, place their own and others' contributions into the chat history, and then deliberate as a group about the best placement for each message. PITCH contains 384 candidate contributions and 1,091 judgments, each marking an ideal turn, an acceptable window, or that a contribution should not appear, from 89 participants engaged in 35 conversations. Evaluating 15 models across 28 configurations, we find that while models can place contributions well when given the entire conversation history, they systematically chime in too early when asked to decide live as the conversation unfolds: best-turn accuracy falls from 57.8% to 19.0%, with nearly half of placements occurring before every participant's acceptable window. In comparison, lay humans deciding live are more accurate (23.7% vs 19.0%), and fewer of their placements are premature (39.7% vs 46.4%). Model reasoning traces show that 93% of intervention justifications cite relevance, while almost none consider waiting. By providing a human-grounded benchmark, our work reveals gaps in agents' ability to integrate into group settings and points towards proactive agents that can reason explicitly about appropriate timing.

With the increasing use of conversational AI (CAI) agents, such as ChatGPT, public concern about their social implications has grown. Understanding these implications requires new knowledge about the increasingly diverse motives underlying CAI use, ranging from instrumental purposes, such as work, to personal purposes, including social support and entertainment. However, little is known about the motivational profiles underlying CAI use, how these profiles relate to personality traits and attachment dimensions, or whether they differ in well-being. To address this gap, we conducted a cross-sectional study with 783 CAI users (Mage = 43.46, SD = 13.58). Drawing on Uses and Gratifications (U & G) Theory, we measured key motivations underlying CAI use, including information seeking, task efficiency, personalization, social interaction, and playfulness, and subjected them to latent profile analysis to uncover distinct motivational profiles. Big Five personality traits (Extraversion, Neuroticism, Openness, Conscientiousness, Agreeableness) and attachment styles (Anxious and Avoidant) were examined as predictors of the user profiles. We measured emotional, social, and psychological well-being to understand if these aspects differed across the various user profiles. We identified four distinct profiles of CAI users: Occasional Information Seekers, Utilitarians, Social Engagers, and All-Round Engagers. Neuroticism, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Attachment anxiety were significant predictors of profile membership. Finally, profile membership was associated with all well-being indicators, with All-Round Engagers reporting the highest well-being across all three dimensions and Social Engagers reporting the lowest emotional and psychological well-being. These findings advance our understanding of who engages with CAI and how, with potential implications for well-being.

Artificial intelligence is changing the conditions under which leaders decide, delegate and exercise authority. Field and experimental evidence shows that generative AI can raise productivity on many knowledge tasks, but it can also lower the quality of decisions when people accept its outputs uncritically. Large practitioner surveys suggest that organizational readiness, including leadership alignment, is lagging behind individual adoption. Organizations have responded mainly by investing in skills: AI literacy, digital capability and updated competency models. This conceptual position paper argues that such investment is necessary but not sufficient. As technology widens what leaders can do, the quality of leadership depends more heavily on the leader's formation: the process through which purpose and identity are clarified and integrated, expressed as a recognizable leadership signature, and refined through ownership of the impact that leadership produces. Drawing on research into leader identity, developmental readiness, leader character, paradox, identity threat and automation bias, the paper defines leadership formation and the formed leader through the four dimensions of the Four Prints Method, a practice-derived framework: purpose, identity, signature and impact. Purpose and identity are treated as the measurable root of formation, signature as its expression and impact as its evidence. It then proposes a construct, grounded adaptability: the capacity to keep purpose, identity and ethical commitments coherent while revising strategies, methods and beliefs about means in response to new evidence. The construct is distinguished from paradox mindset, paradoxical leader behavior, organizational ambidexterity, adaptive leadership, learning agility and authentic leadership. Its proposed mechanism is the source of a leader's grounding. Grounding that rests on role-contingent attributes, such as expertise or position, is expected to make AI-driven disruption feel like a threat to identity, and so to provoke rigid or reactive responses. Grounding that rests on purpose and values is expected to support discriminating adaptation instead. The paper advances five testable propositions, specifies rival explanations and outlines research designs. Its implications for executive development, succession, AI governance and leadership education are each labelled by the strength of evidence behind them. The paper concludes that leader formation should be treated as a necessary, though not sufficient, part of preparing leaders to govern powerful technologies responsibly.

documents.abstract: The capacity of Large Language Models (LLMs) is groundbreaking, given their ability to produce the next most probable words near perfection according to user prompts via chatbots. This represents a capacity for cognitive reasoning in learning by selecting words strategically based on an understanding of context and intent. When an AI model reaches the point where it can organize thoughts and generate structured writing, how deliberate does the ordinary human remain in cognitive engagement and freedom of choice? This paper explicitly examines LLM-assisted writing from a practical co-partner perspective, analyzing its impact on knowledge work, the functioning of overall AI workflows, and its influence on human cognition. Recent studies on human–LLM collaboration, alongside the author's nearly half a decade of practical experience, are presented to substantiate this perspective. Large language models now write a material and growing share of production software, including software that executes regulated financial functions.The empirical literature on their reliability has grown rapidly and is, on its own terms, sophisticated.The governance frameworks that regulated institutions must satisfy were, without exception, written for a different kind of artefact, and in the most consequential recent case, were revised in full knowledge of generative AI and deliberately declined to cover it.Objective.This review synthesises the evidence on the reliability of AI-assisted code generation, on the human factors governing its use, and on the intellectual-property and supply-chain exposures it creates; and determines how that evidence maps onto the model-risk, AI-specific and operational-resilience regimes applicable to regulated software environments.Method.We conducted a systematic literature review following Kitchenham et al. and reported against PRISMA 2020, with a restricted multivocal stratum after Garousi et al. admitting regulatory instruments and supervisory guidance.Studies were appraised on an adapted Dybå-Dingsøyr instrument extended with an item recording whether deployment context or regulatory constraint is characterised.Results.Five findings.First, benchmark performance and field reliability have decoupled: correctness benchmarks are saturated and contamination-prone while defect rates measured in real repositories remain substantial, so the headline capability numbers do not license deployment inferences.Second, security evidence is mixed, controlled model evaluations report high vulnerability rates while several developer studies find little or no security penalty, and the disagreement is explained by unit of analysis rather than by any study being wrong.Third, the most robust human-factors finding is not that assisted code is worse but that developers believe it is better than it is, which relocates the risk from the artefact to the review process.Fourth, package hallucination converts a model reliability property into an attacker-controllable supply-chain channel, and is the one exposure with no human-review mitigation.Fifth, and most consequentially, the April 2026 revision of US interagency model-risk guidance explicitly excludes generative and agentic AI from scope, leaving the primary supervisory framework silent on precisely this class of system. A Systematic Review of AI-Assisted Code Generation in Regulated Software Environments: Reliability, Governance, and ComplianceImplications; David Excel Ozowara Conclusion.We argue that AI-assisted code generation is misclassified when treated as a model-risk problem, because the model produces no decision and enters no inventory; it is better understood as a change to the software development lifecycle's assurance basis.We present the Generated Code Assurance Frame, a five-layer mapping from generation practice to the assurance claim it disturbs, and a research agenda centred on measuring review efficacy rather than generation quality.Citation

documents.abstract: The study aimed to examine the effect of personalized learning through artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics on student engagement and learning outcomes of higher education institutes in Pakistan with implications for Research Integrity at these institutes. Adopting a mixed methods approach, quantitative data gathered from 500 students from an undergraduate science program, with semi structured interviews with 30 students for the qualitative data. The descriptive statistics indicated that the mean engagement scores for those students who have access to AI based personalized learnings were significantly higher than the mean scores of students in traditional learning setting; it is from these that an increase in engagement by the students were observed. There was an improvement in Academic achievement as well, as indicated by higher grade point averages, and improved scores of the formative assessments. The regression analysis results showed that AI (personalized learning) and learning analytics (β = .41; p < .001) were among its most important models that were significant in predicting the variable of academic achievement; the analysis of correlation results showed that there was a good positive correlation between the variables of engagement and academic achievement (r = .63, p < .01). The qualitative results corroborated this as students felt there was a significant increase in motivation, personalized feedback, and adaptive learning pathways as being the most beneficial aspects of the AI integration. Issues were identified that could interfere in successful implementation: Data privacy concerns, uneven access to technology and insufficient faculty preparation. According to this study, personalized learning & learning analytics with AI have proved to be significant drivers of student engagement & academic performance, provided that the ethical issues and infrastructure are sorted out and this may influence the way research integrity and rigor will be upheld within Higher Education Institutions. The findings herein expand the conversation taking place around the role of AI in education and highlight the need to embed learning analytics in a learning design practice, to create inclusive and effective learning spaces.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in higher education, yet the pedagogical field intended to organise its use remains conceptually underdeveloped. This scoping review mapped and synthesised peer-reviewed literature on AI pedagogy in higher education, using teacher education as the primary analytic lens. Following Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting principles, searches were conducted across ten databases and publisher platforms for literature published between 2022 and March 2026. Of 956 records screened, 191 studies were included. Data charting and synthesis combined deductive coding, an a priori codebook, AI-assisted coding in Atlas. ti, and human inductive open coding. Six interrelated themes emerged: AI pedagogy is contextually produced rather than universally defined; conceptualised through pedagogical integration, competence, and borrowed theories rather than a settled standalone theory; enacted mainly through augmentation-oriented practices and generative AI tools; and associated with changing teacher professionalism, ethical mediation, governance, structural constraints, and a rapidly expanding but methodologically uneven evidence base. The review rejects purely technical, universal, or tool-centred models of innovation. Instead, it positions AI pedagogy as a context-specific, human-led, competence-rich, and governance-aware form of teaching in which AI supports planning, feedback, adaptation, and reflection without displacing human educational responsibility, especially within teacher education contexts and programmes.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to analyze and compare design alternatives, yet how design students evaluate AI advice and how such evaluation relates to final design judgments remain insufficiently understood. This study examines the associations among perceived AI interaction conditions, critical evaluation of AI advice, and expert-rated Design Judgment Quality. A cross-sectional study combined a standardized poster comparison task with a post-task questionnaire involving 118 visual communication design students. Participants interacted with Doubao-Seed-2.1-Pro and submitted design choices, rationales, and revision recommendations. Perceived Feedback Diagnosticity, Interaction Controllability, and three critical evaluation activities were measured through post-task self-reports, while Design Judgment Quality was independently assessed by three experts. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was used for hypothesis testing. Feedback Diagnosticity was positively associated with Evidence Verification, Argument Scrutiny, Contextual Fit Evaluation, and Design Judgment Quality. Interaction Controllability was positively associated with Argument Scrutiny and Contextual Fit Evaluation, but not directly with Design Judgment Quality. Among the three evaluation activities, only Argument Scrutiny showed a significant positive association with expert-rated Design Judgment Quality. These findings suggest that AI-assisted design judgment requires attention to both the perceived value of AI feedback and how users examine AI recommendations and their underlying rationales.

This conceptual working paper examines whether the New Human Rights (Neue Menschenrechte, NMR) approach developed by Jean-Pol Martin displays the characteristics of an emerging school of thought.It proposes five analytical criteria: a shared theoretical core, an interconnected vocabulary, a recognizable mode of inquiry, sustained collective activity, and autonomous contributions beyond the founder. Drawing on selected primary texts, publisher descriptions and public practitioner accounts, the paper identifies indications of these features in publications, training activities and distinct applications of the framework.The conceptual architecture connects an organism-based understanding of human beings, six basic need domains, a universal normative commitment to enabling their satisfaction, and a process model linking exploration, information processing, conceptualization and agency. Learning by Teaching (LdL) and human–AI cooperation are situated within this architecture.The article’s specific contribution is to shift attention from an individual theoretical project to the development of a shared intellectual and practical tradition. Within the ongoing sequence of papers on LdL, NMR and human–AI cooperation, it connects the reconstruction of Martin’s work with a prospective collective research programme.The paper distinguishes autonomous development within the project from independent reception outside its originating network. It concludes that “an emerging NMR school of thought” is a defensible interpretation of the documented activities and identifies questions for further conceptual and empirical investigation.Prepared by Jean-Pol Martin in collaboration with ChatGPT. The article includes references and an authorship transparency statement.

This anatomical review systematically dissects Noguer i Alonso's (2026) framework for hybrid workflows integrating human decision makers (H), specified computational procedures (D), and adaptive artificial delegates (A). The paper advances a principled account of agentification, deagentification, automation, and harnessing, grounded in a partial order on delegation profiles rather than scalar autonomy scores, and supported by formal results on permission restriction, invariant preservation, retry exposure, advisory isolation, and the proceduralization gap. While the contribution offers valuable conceptual clarity for task-specific authority allocation in agentic systems, the review identifies limitations in empirical scope (synthetic examples only), the open problem of semantic promotion, and the transferability of formal guarantees to production environments. Implications for AI governance, hybrid intelligence, and institutional design in Global South contexts are discussed.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly investigated as decision-support technologies for supply chain management (SCM), yet their value depends on the nature of the decision, data availability, organisational capability and the methods used to evaluate outcomes. This critical narrative review examines applications across demand forecasting, inventory planning, sourcing, manufacturing, logistics, risk management and sustainability. It brings together relevant peer-reviewed reviews, conceptual contributions and empirical studies, and distinguishes evidence from operational deployments from results reported in literature syntheses or simulations. The literature supports the practical relevance of data-driven prediction, pattern detection and decision augmentation, but it does not establish uniform improvements in cost, forecast accuracy, resilience or environmental performance across settings. Reviewed research also identifies integration costs, fragmented data, process misalignment, model drift, limited transparency and governance concerns as barriers to realising benefits. Recent work on generative AI broadens possible applications to document-intensive processes, synthetic scenarios and interactive decision support, while indicating that field-based validation remains limited. A process-oriented framework is proposed in which analytics inform planning, procurement, manufacturing, distribution and inventory decisions under continuous human oversight. The review argues that useful evaluations should compare AI-supported decisions against relevant operational baselines, account for service levels and cost trade-offs, and document transferability across sectors and resource settings. Future research should prioritise longitudinal field studies, cross-organisational coordination, responsible deployment and context-sensitive applications in emerging economies.
